projects.title: JalTech – E-Commerce Advisory Platform
projects.shortDescription: Advisory module for a Colombian tech distributor that let customers self-serve and advisors act as order proxies — cutting billing time in half.

problem.situation: Order-taking was 100% manual: a customer called an advisor, the advisor wrote the order down by hand, then it was keyed into billing later.
problem.businessContext: Colombia's e-commerce boom (2020–2021) was accelerating, but JalTech's advisors — spread across regions like Chocó — had no digital tools to keep up.
problem.userPain: Advisors spent over 60% of their time on admin instead of selling, and customers had no way to order without waiting for an advisor to be free.
problem.metric: Order-to-billing time → target: cut it dramatically

solution.approach: Built an advisory module: customers could self-serve their own orders, and advisors could act as a proxy — capturing customer data and mounting the order directly in the system, auto-billed.
keyFeatures: Self-service order creation for end customers
Advisor-as-proxy order entry with auto-billing
Automatic order confirmations
Order tracking dashboard

technicalDecisions.decision: Build the module on top of WordPress, integrated with JalTech's existing billing system
technicalDecisions.rationale: Fastest path to shipping without replacing infrastructure the client already depended on
technicalDecisions.tradeoff: Tied future iterations to WordPress's plugin ecosystem, but avoided a costly re-platform

solution.mvpScope: Self-service ordering + advisor-as-proxy flow shipped first; checkout redesign, product descriptions, and mega menu came later as the platform evolved

myRole.title: Product Manager (first formal PM role)
responsibilities: Ran field discovery — visited JalTech regularly to map how advisors and customers actually worked, not how a spec assumed they worked
Educated a pre-agile client on iterative delivery: why 'good in 3 weeks, improved after' beats 'perfect in 6 months'
Prioritized MVP scope around advisor impact first, customer impact second
Trained advisors during rollout and ran a continuous feedback loop to prioritize fixes
keyDecisions: Shipped the advisor-as-proxy flow before full customer self-service, because it unblocked revenue fastest
Built a recurring listening loop with advisors (demos + feedback sessions) instead of a one-time handoff
Held the line on 2-week sprints even when the client pushed for a single big-bang release

metrics.metric1: Billing time: 2–3 hours → 15–30 minutes per order
metrics.metric2: Advisor adoption: feature was actively requested, not just tolerated
metrics.metric3: Engagement: single project → 18+ months of ongoing platform evolution work

results.businessOutcome: 2x faster order-to-billing velocity. Codebulls went from a one-off vendor to JalTech's long-term platform partner, later redesigning checkout, product descriptions, and category navigation.

retrospective.whatWorked: Getting into the field with advisors surfaced constraints — like advisors working from tablets on the road — that never would have shown up in an office meeting.
retrospective.whatDidnt: Early expectation-setting on timelines was harder than expected with a client new to iterative delivery.
retrospective.nextTime: Would formalize the advisor feedback loop from week one instead of building it organically after launch.

projects.title: Raio – Spaced Repetition Language Learning App
projects.shortDescription: A science-backed, non-gamified alternative to Duolingo — mobile flashcards using spaced repetition, shipped on iOS and Android for a YouTube language-learning influencer.

problem.situation: The client had a clear vision in his head — a spaced-repetition learning app — but no spec, no wireframes, and no technical plan.
problem.businessContext: He had built an engaged YouTube audience around learning English and wanted a product that matched his no-nonsense teaching style, not a gamified app.
problem.userPain: Language learners wanted an efficient way to actually retain what they studied, not streaks and badges.
problem.metric: Time-to-market → target: ship on both app stores within a year

solution.approach: Translated the client's vision into Miro wireframes — swipeable flashcards driven by a spaced-repetition algorithm — then handed off to Celerik's design team for high-fidelity design and build.
keyFeatures: Spaced-repetition scheduling engine
Swipe/tap flashcard interaction
Multi-language support
Published on the Apple App Store and Google Play

technicalDecisions.decision: Started with the Google Translate API instead of a premium translation service
technicalDecisions.rationale: Faster and cheaper to ship an MVP
technicalDecisions.tradeoff: The client pushed back mid-project on translation quality, forcing a scope renegotiation that cost 2–3 sprints

solution.mvpScope: Core flashcard engine + spaced repetition + both store submissions; deferred a premium translation provider and social features

myRole.title: Product Manager
responsibilities: Ran discovery in Miro — turned the client's verbal vision into concrete wireframes and user flows
Negotiated scope creep, most notably a mid-project push to swap translation providers
Learned mobile fundamentals from scratch: iOS vs. Android differences, responsive constraints, App Store and Google Play submission mechanics
Used the app herself to validate the learning experience firsthand
keyDecisions: Held the MVP line on the translation-service scope-creep request rather than absorbing an unbudgeted 2–3 sprint detour
Personally tested the product to catch UX confusion before it reached users
Managed the handoff from her wireframes to Celerik's internal design team

metrics.metric1: Shipped on both iOS and Android
metrics.metric2: MVP scope held despite repeated scope-creep pressure
metrics.metric3: First deep mobile-domain project of her career

results.businessOutcome: Delivered a working MVP end-to-end, from discovery wireframes to store submission, for a client with high expectations and a fast timeline.

retrospective.whatWorked: Wireframing everything in Miro upfront gave the client and the team a shared visual language before any code was written.
retrospective.whatDidnt: Scope boundaries weren't documented explicitly enough upfront, which fed the mid-project renegotiation fight.
retrospective.nextTime: Would put a written scope agreement in front of the client before kickoff, not just verbal alignment on wireframes.

projects.title: Gold by Gold – Gold Traceability & Compliance Platform
projects.shortDescription: Centralized platform to legalize and trace gold from three sourcing channels in Colombia through export to Europe — replacing fully manual, audit-vulnerable paperwork.

problem.situation: Gold came in through three very different channels — subsistence mining, recycled jewelry, and industrial mining — each with its own documentation, and none of it centralized.
problem.businessContext: Exporting to Europe legally requires proving where every ounce of gold came from. Manual paperwork couldn't satisfy that bar or scale with volume.
problem.userPain: Five-plus internal teams — tesorería, radicación, cobros, exportaciones, operations — each ran a different undocumented workflow with no shared source of truth.
problem.metric: Regulatory risk → target: audit-ready traceability, near zero risk

solution.approach: Built a centralized platform to collect provider documentation, run gold through a structured legalization workflow, and generate audit-ready traceability reports.
keyFeatures: Centralized document collection per provider across all three sourcing channels
Gold legalization workflow (weigh-in → processing → export documentation)
Inventory dashboard tracking gold bars through each stage
Traceability reporting built for European auditors

technicalDecisions.decision: Pushed the providers/documentation module into production with the tesorería team before the full legalization module was finished
technicalDecisions.rationale: Skeptical, pre-agile founders needed to see the system working with real employees, not another promise
technicalDecisions.tradeoff: Ran the legacy manual process and the new system in parallel during rollout, adding short-term overhead

solution.mvpScope: Providers and document-radication module shipped to production; the legalization module was still in development at handoff, with exports and advanced reporting deferred to a later phase

myRole.title: Product Manager
responsibilities: Ran field discovery in Medellín across five-plus internal stakeholder workflows
Managed two demanding, ~60-year-old founders with no software background and zero patience for theory
Replaced formal spec meetings with twice-weekly, 20-minute live demos and short recorded explainer videos
Pushed for an early production release so founders could see their own employees using the system
Documented decisions and architecture thoroughly for a clean handoff to the next PM
keyDecisions: Chose tangible demos and videos over trying to explain agile methodology to non-technical founders
Released the MVP into production before it was fully complete, to build trust through momentum
Scoped advanced reporting into a later phase to protect the core delivery timeline
Handed the project off cleanly to another PM once scope grew toward a resellable product

results.launched: 2022 (providers/radication module in production; legalization module handed off in progress)
results.businessOutcome: Founders saw enough traction to consider turning the internal platform into a resellable product. The project transitioned to another PM with full documentation of decisions, architecture, and stakeholder relationships.

retrospective.whatWorked: Tangible demos and an early production release converted skeptical founders far faster than any explanation of iterative methodology could have.
retrospective.whatDidnt: The five-plus stakeholder workflows could have been mapped even earlier to avoid mid-project surprises about how different teams actually worked.
retrospective.nextTime: Would build a full stakeholder workflow map in week one, before any wireframing started.

projects.title: Nevermist – Missed Connections & Community Match App
projects.shortDescription: A social app designed to help people reconnect with strangers they encountered in fleeting, real-life moments. Built advanced matching algorithms, location-based check-ins, and in-app chat with monetization strategies.

problem.situation: People frequently have brief, meaningful encounters with strangers (on the street, public transit, cafes) but lack a way to reconnect. Traditional dating apps don't capture this use case.
problem.businessContext: Large untapped market for community connection and authentic social discovery. Competitors (dating apps, social networks) don't address the 'missed connections' problem.
problem.userPain: Users lose potential connections due to lack of tools to describe and find people they briefly encountered. No safe, structured way to break the ice.
problem.metric: User match success rate and engagement with connection requests

solution.approach: Location-based matching platform where users describe visual traits of people they encountered, and an algorithm returns potential matches within proximity. Safe chat interface for connection.
keyFeatures: Flitting Moment Search Algorithm (visual descriptors: height, hair, skin tone, gender, clothing + location & time)
Connection Requests + In-App Chat
Location-based Check-ins (geolocation radius calculations, integrated with retail data)
Profile Creation & Privacy Settings
Scalable Matching Algorithm v2 (flexible matching for higher engagement)
Monetization Features (unlimited chats, premium visibility, location perks)

technicalDecisions.decision: Real-time geolocation database integration + proximity-based fallback matching logic
technicalDecisions.rationale: Initial strict visual matching created too-few results. Flexible fallback algorithm increased match quality and user engagement significantly.
technicalDecisions.tradeoff: Added complexity to matching logic, but trade-off paid off in retention metrics

solution.mvpScope: Core matching, profile creation, chat, check-ins. Deferred: social features, API integrations for advanced geolocation

myRole.title: Product Manager
responsibilities: Led product discovery with design team (user personas, full user journey mapping)
Facilitated ideation and alignment between founders and UX team
Defined technical and functional requirements with developers
Translated UX flows into actionable user stories and epics
Worked with client to define system logic, data models, and matching rules
Owned all agile rituals (sprint planning, backlog grooming, stakeholder demos, retrospectives)
Explored and prototyped monetization strategies
keyDecisions: Switched from strict to flexible matching algorithm based on early user testing feedback
Prioritized safety/moderation features over feature velocity
Designed freemium monetization model (3 free messages, then $1.99/additional message)

metrics.matchAccuracy: Flexible matching returned 3x more usable results than strict algorithm
metrics.engagement: Users completed match process and sent initial message
metrics.adoption: Early user base retention improved with chat monetization features

results.businessOutcome: Successfully delivered fully functional MVP with advanced matching, profile management, geolocation, and chat. Product continues to evolve with client's internal team.

retrospective.whatWorked: Early UX testing caught matching algorithm issues before full development. User safety features built trust from day one.
retrospective.whatDidnt: Initial matching logic was too rigid. Should have done more algorithmic testing in discovery phase.
retrospective.nextTime: Would prototype matching algorithm variants earlier. Would involve data science earlier to stress-test proximity calculations.

projects.title: Colony Cooks – Ghost Kitchens & Corporate Catering Platform
projects.shortDescription: Multi-role platform enabling customers to order food from ghost kitchens, companies to organize catering with subsidies, and kitchen teams to manage orders and preparation in real-time.

problem.situation: Colony Cooks operates ghost kitchens in LA but lacked a unified platform for order routing, corporate meal management, and kitchen workflow optimization. Orders were tracked manually.
problem.businessContext: Ghost kitchen market growing but fragmented. Companies need efficient catering solutions. Kitchen teams need real-time visibility.
problem.userPain: Customers had no single ordering interface. Companies couldn't configure subsidized team meals. Kitchen staff spent time manually organizing orders instead of preparing food.
problem.metric: Order fulfillment time, order accuracy, kitchen efficiency

solution.approach: Three integrated platforms: B2C ordering, B2B corporate catering with subsidy controls, and kitchen manager portal with real-time order tracking.
keyFeatures: B2C Ordering Platform (browse menus, customize toppings, place orders, auto-routing to kitchens)
B2B Corporate Catering (admin invites employees, sets subsidies partial/full, delivery/pickup options, individual personalization)
Kitchen Manager Portal (real-time order tracking, filter/print/status updates, quantities/ingredients/instructions visibility)
Payment Integration (Stripe)
Multi-role permission system (customers, companies, kitchen admins)

technicalDecisions.decision: Separate backend for each role type vs. monolith with role-based permissions
technicalDecisions.rationale: Kitchen Display System (KDS) tablets needed different data model and permissions than customer apps
technicalDecisions.tradeoff: More complex infrastructure, but enabled real-time order updates and kitchen optimization

solution.mvpScope: All three platforms (B2C, B2B, Kitchen Manager). Full integration with Stripe and email. Deferred: mobile apps, advanced analytics

myRole.title: Product Manager
responsibilities: Led end-to-end product delivery, coordinating frontend, backend, QA, and client
Owned and maintained full product backlog in Jira
Worked with designer and developers to define features for each user role
Created user stories with detailed acceptance criteria and user flow documentation
Facilitated sprint planning, QA cycles, UAT sessions, and go-live preparation
Collaborated with QA (Doralys) on regression checklists and feature-by-feature testing
keyDecisions: Prioritized kitchen workflow efficiency over early monetization features
Chose to observe real kitchen operations before designing manager portal (UX research)
Deferred mobile apps to ensure desktop web version was rock-solid for production use

metrics.qaValidation: All features passed complete regression testing
metrics.teamAccuracy: Kitchen teams tracked orders with zero discrepancies in UAT

results.businessOutcome: Fully functional MVP across three platforms. Client paused product internally post-launch but all scope was completed and deployed. Set foundation for future catering platform expansion.

retrospective.whatWorked: Observing real kitchen operations was crucial. UX research sessions with kitchen staff caught workflow pain points. UAT process was thorough.
retrospective.whatDidnt: Underestimated complexity of cost breakdown logic between customer and company subsidies. Should have involved finance earlier.
retrospective.nextTime: Would do Phase 2 planning (mobile apps, advanced analytics) in parallel to reduce time-to-impact. Would prototype cost logic before full build.

projects.title: PricePicks – Free-to-Play Game Mode & Seasonal Drops
projects.shortDescription: Free-to-play mode for a leading fantasy sports app, letting it legally expand into non-paid states with streaks and event-based minigames instead of real-money betting.

problem.situation: PricePicks operated in paid U.S. states, but regulatory restrictions on monetary betting blocked expansion into non-paid states.
problem.businessContext: The company needed a Free-to-Play (FTP) version that kept the core game's engagement without involving money, to reach new markets legally.
problem.userPain: Users in non-paid states had no way to engage with the core game experience at all.
problem.metric: User base expansion into non-paid states without legal risk

solution.approach: Built a free-to-play mode around daily picks, streaks, leaderboards, and event-based 'Drops' minigames tied to real-world sports and pop-culture moments.
keyFeatures: Daily Pick Game: choose one of 10 daily cards, make an Over/Under prediction
Live scoring during the actual game
Streak tracking and leaderboard competition
Themed 'Drops' minigames tied to events (NFL Combine, Golden Globes, etc.)
Bonus streak mechanics ("Flex Friday", "Taco Tuesday", "Goblin Picks")

technicalDecisions.decision: Ran moderated live user interviews and A/B tests before locking UI decisions
technicalDecisions.rationale: A fully staffed UX research team meant decisions could be data-driven instead of opinion-driven
technicalDecisions.tradeoff: Slower to ship individual UI changes, but higher confidence each change actually improved usability

solution.mvpScope: Daily pick game, streaks, leaderboard, and first seasonal Drop shipped; deferred an expanded Drop calendar and deeper personalization

myRole.title: Product Manager
responsibilities: Coordinated cross-functionally across Marketing, Research, Design, internal devs, and DualBoot
Gathered requirements and kept the roadmap aligned across teams
Supported the design team with clear problem definitions and success metrics
Participated in live moderated user interviews and unassisted usability testing
Ran sprint planning, backlog triage, and delivery QA
keyDecisions: Prioritized entertainment mechanics (streaks, Drops) over betting-adjacent framing to stay compliant
Used real usage metrics (click-through, adoption, retention) instead of opinion to decide what to keep or cut
Adopted Linear for backlog and roadmap management for the team's speed and clarity

results.launched: 2024 (FTP mode); Drops program continued through May 2025

metrics.metric2: FTP mode well received, laid foundation for long-term engagement
metrics.metric3: Established a repeatable model for event-based 'Drops' minigames

results.businessOutcome: Enabled the company to expand its user base into new states without legal risk, backed by a fully data-driven UX research process.

retrospective.whatWorked: Live moderated interviews and A/B testing gave the team empathy-driven, data-backed confidence in each design decision.
retrospective.whatDidnt: Coordinating across five-plus teams (Marketing, Research, Design, internal dev, DualBoot) sometimes slowed decision cycles.
retrospective.nextTime: Would set up a single shared source of truth for research findings earlier to speed up cross-team alignment.

projects.title: National Media – AI Media Buying Automation (MediaBuyer)
projects.shortDescription: A two-stage AI pipeline — Google Gemini + LangGraph — that automates TV media buying: extracting rate cards, matching audience data, and generating constraint-validated media buys with a human-in-the-loop review step.

problem.situation: TV media buying was manual: planners spent hours extracting rate-card data, matching programs against audience data, and hand-building buys against strict business constraints.
problem.businessContext: The team needed to ship ahead of a political media-buying cycle deadline, while stitching together three-plus external systems: Google Gemini, VideoAMP/Snowflake, and Azure infrastructure.
problem.userPain: Manual matching was slow and error-prone, and there was no systematic way to validate a proposed buy against rules like GRP targets, CPP limits, daypart shares, and budget tolerance.
problem.metric: Media buying speed → target: roughly 2x faster than manual

solution.approach: Built two independent, event-driven LangGraph pipelines: Stage 1 (Enrich Programs) extracts and matches rate-card data against audience data using AI reconnaissance; Stage 2 (Build Optimal Media Buy) generates a buy and iteratively validates it against business constraints.
keyFeatures: Rate card upload (CSV/XLSX/XML)
14-node enrichment pipeline: Gemini extraction + VideoAMP/Snowflake audience matching
Confidence-scored matchmaking review CSV for human validation before a buy is generated
8-node buy-generation pipeline with iterative constraint refinement (up to 3 passes)
XML/CSV export for import into Strata
Real-time status polling for media planners

technicalDecisions.decision: Two independent pipelines instead of one monolithic flow
technicalDecisions.rationale: Lets either stage retry or restart on failure without losing the other stage's completed work
technicalDecisions.tradeoff: More orchestration complexity up front, but far more resilient to the failure modes inherent in three-plus external integrations

solution.mvpScope: Rate card upload through Stage 1 and Stage 2, human-in-the-loop review, and XML/CSV export; deferred a full history/reporting view (hardcoded for UAT 1.0) and multi-market batching

myRole.title: Product Manager
responsibilities: Defined confidence thresholds for AI outputs (below 70% → routed to manual review) instead of treating AI output as simply done or not done
Translated media-buying terminology — GRP, CPP, daypart shares, rate cards — into concrete validator rules engineering could build against
Designed the human-in-the-loop matchmaking review step so planners validate matches before a buy is generated
Worked with architects on contingency plans — model fallback, local caching, retry queues — across all three external integrations
Aligned a roughly 10-person, cross-repo team spanning frontend, backend, and AI automation
Chose to ship documented known issues transparently rather than delay launch or hide gaps
keyDecisions: Set the 70% confidence threshold gating automatic matches vs. human-reviewed ones
Scoped out multi-market batching and full history reporting to protect the June 2026 launch date
Prioritized reliability — audit trails, fallbacks, retry logic — over adding more automation features

metrics.metric1: Media buying speed: roughly 2x faster than manual (preliminary)
metrics.metric3: Every pipeline run logged for audit and debugging

results.businessOutcome: Shipped a working AI-automated media-buying pipeline on schedule, with two known issues documented publicly (a frontend validation gap and a status-refresh bug) and scheduled for the next iteration rather than rushed or hidden.

retrospective.whatWorked: Designing for AI uncertainty from day one — confidence thresholds plus mandatory human review — avoided a 'trust the AI blindly' failure mode.
retrospective.whatDidnt: Some constraint-validation edge cases only surfaced once the AI was generating buys against real rate cards, not during early testing.
retrospective.nextTime: Would build the constraint validator and a larger synthetic test dataset earlier, before the AI-generation pipeline was fully wired up.

projects.title: Awardees – Resource Management & Project Planning Platform
projects.shortDescription: Multi-tenant SaaS platform for organizations to plan projects, allocate people, and manage resource requests from a single system.

problem.situation: The client had no centralized way to plan projects, assign roles, track availability, or manage internal resource requests.
problem.businessContext: The long-term vision is a multi-tenant platform that scales beyond a single client to support broader internal team coordination.
problem.userPain: Teams couldn't see resource availability or allocation in real time, making planning and requests slow and error-prone.
problem.metric: Clean, testable MVP backlog covering core resource-planning functionality

solution.approach: Built four core modules — Projects, People, Requests, and User Management — on a role-based, multi-tenant-ready architecture.
keyFeatures: People directory: profiles, documents, roles, availability, skills, allocation history
Projects management: project records, phases, resource assignment by role
Requests module: structured workflow for initiating and approving resource assignments
Availability & allocation planning with over/under-allocation visibility
Role-based permissions matrix (Admins, Supervisors, Read-only)

technicalDecisions.decision: Designed the data model and permissions system for multi-tenancy from day one, even though the first release serves a single client
technicalDecisions.rationale: Retrofitting multi-tenancy later would mean rebuilding data isolation and permission logic from scratch
technicalDecisions.tradeoff: More upfront design work before the first client-facing feature shipped

solution.mvpScope: People, Projects, Requests, and User Management modules; deferred a full multi-tenant onboarding flow for additional organizations

myRole.title: Product Manager
responsibilities: Helped define the initial MVP scope based on business needs and technical feasibility
Structured and maintained the backlog in Azure DevOps, split into small, testable, role-specific tasks
Worked directly with the client and designers to shape UX flows and user journeys
Defined system logic, field behavior, and validation rules across key modules
Supported AI integration planning for role recommendations based on user attributes and onboarding data
keyDecisions: Designed the People and Projects detail views around tabbed navigation for structured data
Chose to plan for multi-tenant scale from the MVP instead of retrofitting later
Aligned frontend/backend QA priorities each sprint to keep the backlog testable

results.launched: Ongoing (MVP modules delivered, platform in active development)

metrics.metric1: Delivered a clean, testable MVP backlog covering core functionality
metrics.metric2: Four core modules shipped: People, Projects, Requests, User Management
metrics.metric3: AI-assisted role-matching logic scoped for onboarding

results.businessOutcome: Built stakeholder trust and alignment by documenting and validating each interaction flow, setting up the platform to scale into a true multi-tenant product.

retrospective.whatWorked: Designing permissions and data isolation for multi-tenancy from the start avoided costly rework later.
retrospective.whatDidnt: Still refining how much of the long-term multi-tenant vision to lock in early vs. leave flexible.
retrospective.nextTime: Would map the full permissions matrix across all planned tenant types even earlier.
